text:
Jacek Karpiński was born in 1927 in Turin, Italy, into a family of Polish intellectuals and alpinists. His father, Adam Karpiński, was a prominent aeronautic engineer and inventor, while his mother, Wanda Czarnocka-Karpińska, was a respected physician and later Dean of the University of Physical Education in Warsaw. The family moved to Warsaw in 1934, where both parents worked in academia and engineering.
During World War II, Karpiński joined the Home Army at age 14, serving in the Gray Ranks. He was severely injured during a sabotage operation in 1943, losing both eyes and facing the threat of hand amputation. After recovery, he continued his resistance work, including participating in the Warsaw Uprising, where he was wounded but survived.
Post-war, he attended local high school in Radomsko, completed his education, and moved to Łódź to study at the Faculty of Electro-Mechanical Sciences. He later graduated from Warsaw University of Technology in 1951.
Karpiński's career in engineering began with the development of the AAH — Analytical Analyzer of Harmonics, a device he built with his friend Józef Lityński to improve weather forecasting. His breakthrough achievement was the construction of AKAT-1, the world's first differential equations analyzer based on transistors, developed at the Polish Academy of Sciences. The machine was praised for its innovative design and aesthetic appeal, with artistic panels by leading Polish artists.
In 1960, Karpiński was awarded the UNESCO scholarship to study in the United States, where he visited major technological centers and met leading computer scientists. After returning, he designed the Polish perceptron, one of the first such devices in the world. Later, he developed the KAR-65, a computer with high-speed performance and modularity, which became the fastest Polish computer at the time.
Despite facing political challenges and financial constraints, Karpiński's work was recognized with numerous honors, including the Officer's Cross of Polonia Restituta in 2009 and the Commander's Cross of Polonia Restituta in 2010. He retired from active work in 1978 and later moved to Switzerland, where he worked on Nagra tape recorders. He died in 2010 in Wrocław, Poland.
